Give permwatch Full Disk Access once

Without it macOS asks separately for Downloads, Desktop, Documents and every other folder, and permissions and login items stay invisible. With this single permission permwatch can check every folder and disk; it only reads, never changes your files. System Settings › Privacy & Security › Full Disk Access › turn on permwatch.
%1$@ sent a user name or password to %2$@ without encryption. Anyone on the same network (a café Wi-Fi, for example) could read it.
Change this password, and change it everywhere you reuse it. Use the service only over https://, or stop using it if it doesn’t offer encryption.
%1$@ is talking to %2$@, a %3$@ service. These services collect what you do in the app and often share it with advertisers.
Not dangerous, but it costs privacy. Look for “analytics”, “usage data” or “improve the product” in the app’s settings and turn it off; in browsers, a content blocker helps.
%1$@ is using plain HTTP with %2$@. The connection is not encrypted: the pages, files and data can be read or changed on the way.
Don’t enter passwords or personal data here. If it’s a website, try https:// instead. If an app downloads updates this way, ask its developer or look for an alternative.
%@ is an old protocol without encryption: everything, including logins, travels as readable text.
Switch to the encrypted version in the app’s account settings: SFTP instead of FTP, SSH instead of Telnet, and SSL/TLS for mail (ports 993, 995, 465).
Port %@ is often used by hacking tools and remote-control malware. Some legitimate programs use it too.
If you don’t recognise the app, check it with VirusTotal and quit it from Running Apps.
%1$@ is trying to open a connection to your Mac on port %2$@. A sharing service or server on your Mac may be reachable from the network.
Turn on the firewall (Security section) and switch off sharing services you don’t use in System Settings › General › Sharing.
%1$@ is starting an encrypted connection to %2$@. Only the site name is visible; the content stays hidden. Encryption doesn’t tell whether the site is safe; check the name if you don’t recognise it.
Encrypted traffic between %1$@ and %2$@: nobody on the network can read the content. Encryption doesn’t prove the server is trustworthy; if you know the app, this is expected.
An encrypted remote login (SSH). Someone is logging in to a computer, or into yours.
Fine if you started it. If the connection comes in to your Mac and you didn’t expect it, turn off Remote Login in System Settings › General › Sharing.
The name %@ does not exist. The occasional typo is normal.
If one app asks for many random-looking names that don’t exist, it may be malware searching for its control server: check that app.
The address book of the internet (DNS) answered: these are the server addresses for %@. Completely normal.
%1$@ is looking up the address of %2$@ before connecting. Every connection starts like this.
Devices on your local network announcing themselves (printers, TVs, AirPlay, other Macs). Normal.
Devices on your network asking “who has this address?” so they can talk to each other. Normal.
Network control messages, such as ping or “address unreachable”. Normal unless there are huge amounts.
Your Mac getting its network address from the router. Normal.
Your Mac setting its clock from a time server. Normal.
A connection was closed abruptly. This happens often (a tab closed, a server busy) and is usually harmless.
%1$@ is opening a new connection to %2$@ (port %3$@).
Data between %1$@ and %2$@. Nothing unusual was found in this packet.
%1$@ sent %2$@ to %3$@ but received only %4$@. Apps that back up or sync files do this; other apps normally don’t.
If you didn’t expect this app to upload files, quit it and check it with VirusTotal.
Share of traffic nobody on the network can read. Higher is better.

System Integrity Protection stops malware from changing macOS itself. It should never be off on a normal Mac. Turn it back on from Recovery mode with “csrutil enable”.
Gatekeeper checks that apps come from identified developers and were scanned by Apple before they open. With it off, any downloaded program can run without a warning.
FileVault encrypts your disk. Without it, anyone who takes your Mac can read your files by removing the disk or starting from another drive.
The firewall blocks unwanted incoming connections, for example on a café or hotel Wi-Fi. Turning it on doesn’t slow anything down and doesn’t affect your normal browsing.
XProtect is Apple’s built-in malware scanner. Its definitions look out of date; keep automatic security updates on so it learns about new threats.
Automatic security updates install fixes for actively exploited holes, often within days. Turn on “Install Security Responses and system files”.
Unsigned programs that start automatically, or apps that got sensitive permissions in an unusual way. Each one has its own explanation; mark the ones you recognise as trusted.
Programs running from unusual places, pretending to be system processes, or whose file was deleted after starting. Open each one to see why and quit it if you don’t know it.

Downloaded apps or installers that Apple’s Gatekeeper would reject, or whose quarantine mark was removed so macOS won’t check them. Don’t open them unless you trust the source; move them to the Trash otherwise.
Unsigned programs connecting to the internet or waiting for incoming connections. Legitimate developer tools do this too, but malware does it all the time.
